title: Why Bc4: the bishop, the f7 target and the first moves
question: Why does White put the bishop on c4, what is Black aiming at in reply, and what does each of the first six moves set up?
outcomes: Names the square the bishop on c4 targets (f7), counts its attackers and defenders, and says why the count changes after Black castles
Gives the job of each of the first six moves of the Italian Game on a board
Names Black's three usual replies (Giuoco Piano, Two Knights, Paris Defence) with their counts, and what each chooses; knows Be7 as a rare quiet try
Explains why a premature knight move to g5 loses a piece against the bishop reply and works only when the knight is defended
Reads our master and online counts with their sample sizes and says what they do not show
Says what the c3 plan and the d3 plan each aim for, and where each side's pieces go

steps.caption: You are Black, to move. White's bishop on c4 looks down a long diagonal toward a pawn at the far end. What would you play here, and why? Decide before you read on.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks the pawn on f7: the bishop on c4.
One black piece defends f7: the king.
No black piece is loose (attacked and undefended).

steps.prompt: Write your move for Black and the reason for it. Then name the square White's bishop is aiming at.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Why does White put the bishop on c4, what is Black aiming at in reply, and what does each of the first six moves set up? You will name the target and its guards, give the job of every opening move, list Black's usual replies, and say when the pressure on f7 is real. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis, [R] recalled.

**Who chooses the bishop on c4?** Our data, at the moment White picks a bishop square. Masters (both players 2500+): b5 in 26,563 of 46,776 listed games, c4 in 13,320. Online, rated 1500-1700: c4 in 44,159 of 105,450 visits, b5 in 20,808. Counts show choices, not quality. [H] Many amateurs prefer c4 because the bishop's aim is visible without calculating. [R] Giuoco Piano is Italian for quiet game.

steps.prompt: The [H] above is a guess. Do you agree? Write one other reason a club player might pick c4 over b5.

steps.text: **Why 3.Bc4 is a classical choice.** [H] It suits a player who likes a clear plan: develop, castle, then strike in the centre. Club players enjoy that the aim is visible; some masters choose it for a slow game with long manoeuvres, as later boards show. [I] The two totals above differ because 13,320 counts White's choices at move three, while 13,329, used further on, counts every game that reaches the position, transpositions included.

steps.caption: At the start, the only guard of the pawn on f7 is the king, and the only guard of f2 is the king. Which of White's pieces could join an attack on f7 first? Keep that question in mind.

claims.statement: Only one black piece guards f7: the king.

steps.caption: The pawn on e6 shuts the diagonal: the bishop touches e6 and never reaches f7. [S] Our sheet of Lasker's Common Sense in Chess (lecture 6) notes that the French Defence's e6 pawn also blocks White's bishop line toward f7. First pawn moves leave lasting marks.

White guards e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal of the bishop on c1.
Black develops the bishop and removes the last piece between the king and the rook.

steps.caption: Black has castled: the king and the rook on f8 now both guard f7, and one bishop attacks it. Count: one attacker against two defenders. The pressure has become a nuisance, not a threat.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks f7.
Two black pieces defend f7.

steps.text: **When f7 is a target.** [I] Early in the game f7 is weakest because only the king guards it. Once a rook arrives, one attacker is not enough, and two are no longer enough on their own. [H] After castling, the bishop's pressure mostly limits Black's choices. Ask each time: who guards f7 now, and who can arrive before I strike?

steps.caption: The first six moves of the Italian Game, one purpose each. Step through and say what each move prepares.

line.say: White claims the centre and opens lines for the queen and the bishop on f1.
Black answers in kind: the same claim, and the two pawns now face each other.
The knight develops and attacks e5, which Black should protect or counter.
Black defends e5 with a developing move instead of a pawn move.
The bishop develops, leaves f1 free for castling, and aims at f7.
Black mirrors it: the bishop develops and aims at f2, guarded only by the king.

claims.statement: After the third move one white piece attacks e5.
After the fourth move one black piece defends e5.
After the fifth move the bishop attacks f7.
After the fifth move f1 is empty.
After the fifth move g1 is empty.
After the sixth move one black piece (the bishop) attacks f2.

steps.prompt: Sort the first six moves by their main job. Moves in order: e4, e5, Nf3, Nc6, Bc4, Bc5. Some moves do two jobs; choose the main one. One of the options may not fit any of the six.

steps.text: **Our reading of the six.** [I] The pawns claim the centre. The four piece moves develop and aim at once: one knight hits e5, the other guards it, the bishops point at f7 and f2. None is about king safety; castling is next. [S] Capablanca (Chess Fundamentals) advised developing fast, knights before bishops; Lasker (Common Sense in Chess) wanted every move to add working power. [I] Both fit our six moves.

steps.caption: Reply one: the mirror. The bishop develops on the same kind of diagonal and aims at f2, which only the White king guards. This is the Giuoco Piano, the name our opening data gives it.

line.say: The bishop develops with an aim at f2: the same idea White used, from the other side.

claims.statement: After Bc5 one black piece attacks f2.
Only one white piece (the king) defends f2.

steps.caption: Reply two: counterattack. The knight does not defend anything; it attacks e4, which no White piece guards. White must answer at once. This is the Two Knights Defence.

line.say: The knight attacks the pawn on e4 and leaves the king's bishop at home.

claims.statement: After Nf6 the pawn on e4 is attacked and undefended.
The knight on f6 does not guard f7: only the king does.

steps.caption: Reply three: solid. The pawn on d6 supports e5 and keeps the centre closed; our data call it the Paris Defence. It blocks the c8 bishop and leaves f7 with one guard. Engine (depth 16): about +0.4 for White here against about +0.2 after the other two replies, a small gap shown as evidence under recorded settings, not a verdict.

claims.statement: One black piece (the king) defends f7.
The engine rates the position a little better for White (depth 16).
c3, d4, castling and Nc3 are all sound.
The pawn on d6 guards e5.

steps.text: **Black's replies in our data** [V, recounted]. Masters, 13,329 games after the bishop move: Giuoco Piano 7,134 (White won 2,362, drew 3,115, Black won 1,657); Two Knights 5,911 (2,172, 2,279, 1,460); Paris (d6) 216; the rare bishop to e7 59. Online, 1500-1700, 47,772 games: Giuoco Piano 15,037; Two Knights 14,696; h6 7,300; d6 3,547; bishop to e7 1,805. Counts show choices; 59 games prove nothing about a result.

steps.caption: After the sharp knight move f7 is attacked twice and defended once, yet the best reply is not to guard it. Black strikes in the centre and hits the bishop. Of 579 master games listed here, 563 went d5.

steps.caption: The centre is locked head to head. No file is open, and each side has four pawns on each wing. What is undecided is who moves the d-pawn, and when. The next two boards show the two choices.

claims.statement: No file is open or half-open.

steps.caption: The open choice. A pawn to c3 prepares d4, and if the centre pawns are traded the position opens. Note the files: after the exchange the e-file is half-open for Black and the c-file for White.

line.say: The pawn will support the d4 break by attacking that square.

White strikes at the centre: the pawn attacks e5 and the bishop on c5.
Black takes; the e5 pawn is gone and the e-file changes character.
White rebuilds a pawn on d4. The e-file is now half-open for Black, the c-file for White.

claims.statement: After the five moves the e-file is half-open for Black and the c-file for White, and no file is open.
After c3 the pawn on c3 attacks d4.

steps.caption: The closed choice. A pawn to d3 guards e4 for good and keeps the centre shut. The price is time and space; the gain is safety. Masters chose d3 in 1,964 of 7,112 listed games here.

line.say: The pawn guards e4 and frees the bishop on c1.
Black develops and attacks e4 again.
White prepares d4 even so, keeping both options open.
Black supports e5 with a pawn, and the centre stays closed.

steps.caption: The d4 plan, continued. White now owns d4 and e4 and has a half-open c-file; Black has a half-open e-file. The centre is the target of both sides: Black checks to gain time, then hits it with a pawn. [I] Neither side is clearly better; the engine (depth 16) is close to level.

line.say: Black checks. The bishop attacks the king and eyes the pawn that supports e4.
White blocks with the bishop; a knight block would walk into a capture on e4.
Black trades off White's dark-squared bishop.
The knight recaptures and stays developed.
Black strikes the centre at once: the pawn attacks both e4 and the bishop. This is the break the whole line was heading for.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position close to level (depth 16).
After the check, the trade and the pawn break a black pawn attacks c4.
White has the half-open c-file and Black the half-open e-file.

steps.caption: The d3 plan. Nothing breaks the centre yet; both sides improve their pieces. White's bishop avoids a pawn attack from b5 by stepping back to b3 and keeps the f7 diagonal; Black keeps the bishop alive on a7 on the f2 diagonal. [I] The plan is manoeuvring, not a quick attack.

line.say: White's bishop retreats before a black pawn can hit it, and keeps its aim at f7.
Black's bishop keeps the diagonal toward f2 and avoids being traded.
The rook supports e4, the pawn the whole structure hangs on.
Black castles; the rook on f8 now also guards f7.

claims.statement: The bishop on b3 still attacks f7.
Black has castled kingside.

steps.caption: The d3 plan, continued: the knight reroutes. From d2 it goes to f1, then to g3 or e3, where it supports e4 and prepares ideas on f5 or d5. [H] The reroute costs time but loses nothing while the centre stays shut. Black's pawn move asks White's pieces a question about g5, nothing more.

line.say: The knight leaves b1 for d2 so that the c1 bishop and the pawns keep their lines.
Black stops bishop and knight ideas on g5 before they start.
The knight heads for g3 or e3 on its way to the kingside.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position about level (depth 16).
After the reroute White's knight stands on f1.

steps.text: **Two plans, one idea each.** [I] With c3, White wants the d4 break and a big centre; Black's answer is to hit that centre with d5. With d3, White keeps the centre shut and reroutes pieces; Black keeps the bishop on a7 and waits for d5 or a trade. [H] Club players find the shut centre easier to play, because fewer tactics appear. The shape of the pawns tells you which plan you are in.

steps.text:
**Count, then check three things.** [I] A count of two against one is a starting point, not a verdict.
- Can a defender still arrive, as a castling rook can? If not, good.
- Are my attackers safe, unlike the loose knight? If so, good.
- Does the capture win material or only trade? It must win.
When all three come out your way, the target is real; otherwise it is only pressure.

steps.caption: The mirror image. Black can pile onto f2 the same way: the bishop on c5 and the knight on g4 attack it twice and only the king defends it. But it is White's move, so White strikes first on f7. Counting both targets matters.

steps.text: **A common first reaction.** [H] Black treats the pressure on f7 as a threat to answer at once. The favourite way online is the pawn move h6, called the Anti-Fried Liver Defence in our data (7,300 of 47,772 games at 1500-1700). Engine (depth 16): about half a pawn below the best replies, a small concession, not a blunder. The next item tests it.

steps.caption: After 3...h6 White simply takes the centre. Black has spent a move on a threat that was not yet a threat, and the engine (depth 16) gives White a somewhat larger edge than after the developing replies: a small concession.

steps.text: **What to remember.** The bishop on c4 aims at f7, guarded only by the king. Each early move develops and aims. Black's replies: the mirror, the counterattack and the quiet solid pawn, with counts. A count of two against one is only a start: look for arriving defenders and loose attackers. Castling dissolves the target. The centre is undecided: c3 aims for d4, d3 keeps it shut.
